title: Who Feeds Whom
short: It is Rob's birthday lunch. You are under a grapevine on Sofokleous, and the loudest thing on the street is the cutlery. From three o'clock that quiet becomes the law: a police regulation forbids music and loud talk until half past five, and today is the last day of the summer rule. Each twenty-seventh of August, a few lanes away, women carry cakes and lists of names into the church of Saint Fanourios, and each cake feeds at least nine people. Pindar says the first Rhodians forgot the fire for their first sacrifice; here is one still working, in a baking tin. Eat slowly. When Rob's track moves you on, the bazaar street climbs north to the pink mosque; the next track starts under its minaret.
long:
It is Rob's birthday. You are under a grapevine on Sofokleous, and the loudest thing on the street is the cutlery. From three o'clock this quiet stops being manners and becomes the law: a police regulation of nineteen ninety-six forbids music and loud conversation from three until half past five, and today, the last day of September, is the last day of the summer rule. An Athens paper says the penalty can be a few months in jail. The silence is an institution, and so is the table: a Rhodian meal has always settled who feeds whom.

Start with a cake. On the twenty-seventh of August, at the church of Saint Fanourios a few lanes from here, it is mostly women who come, carrying trays of cakes and slips of paper with lists of names. The saint is asked to reveal what is missing, an object, a job, a spouse, a diagnosis, and the cake is the payment: oil and no eggs, an odd number of ingredients, seven like the sacraments, or nine. The priest blesses it and it is shared with at least nine people, with a wish that God forgive the saint's sinful mother, which is a folk touch the Church has never formally held. Pindar says the first Rhodians hurried up their hill to build Athena her altar and forgot the fire, and Diodorus adds that at Lindos her altar stayed fireless for centuries. Here is a fireless offering, still working, in a baking tin. The three nights of music behind the church, put on with a local association that calls itself the Knights of the Old Town, are a panigyri, the ancient word panegyris said the modern way: a whole community feasting at its sanctuary, with a new saint on the door.

The dead eat too. At every memorial, the third day, the ninth, the fortieth, on through the third year, the family brings kollyva, boiled wheat with pomegranate seeds, almonds and cinnamon, moulded into a mound the shape of a grave under powdered sugar. The priest blesses it and everyone present eats a spoonful. Wheat has paid for more than the dead here. About a hundred and sixty years before Christ, King Eumenes of Pergamon gave Rhodes two hundred and eighty thousand measures of grain, to be sold, the money lent out at interest, and the interest to pay the schoolmasters. Polybius sniffed that a city so rich should not beg for its teachers' pay. Wheat into cash into teachers: hold that thought for the library at the top of the bazaar.

A few lanes east, in the Jewish quarter, the week ran on a different table. Thursday night the women started cooking for the Sabbath. On Friday, when the work was done, the family went to the Turkish bath, the banyo turko. Saturday night came stories of Djoha, the trickster the Turks knew as Nasreddin Hoca. At Purim children went house to house with plates of sweets and a blessing: may you live like fresh water, may your house be as full as an egg. At Passover the door was opened and the family sang out that all who are hungry should come and eat. This week is Sukkot, the festival of huts roofed with palm and myrtle, and among the community's own dishes is palamida, which is bonito, and it may well be on your plate today.

Now the kitchen. Last year just over a quarter of Greek hotels hired workers from outside the European Union, and the institute that counted them names housing as a main cause: the rooms a waiter might rent are let by the night to visitors. Giorgos Chotzoglou, who leads the tourism workers' federation, says only one hotel in ten and one catering business in twenty applies the collective agreement, that the worker is not a machine, and that the seasonal unemployment benefit needs a hundred insurance stamps from a single season. The person bringing your plate is doing arithmetic this week: did the summer give me my hundred. When Rob's track moves you on, it goes north and up the bazaar street, the one the Jews called up at the judge's, to the pink mosque. The next track starts under the minaret.

title: The Endowment and the Clock
short: In front of the rose-pink mosque, find the small domed fountain on eight columns. The columns are older than the mosque, and the water is for washing before prayer. An Ottoman town ran on endowments: a family locked away shops and orchards, and the rents paid for a fountain, a teacher, a library. The library across the lane is one, endowed in seventeen ninety-two by a man from a village four kilometres south who held the sultan's stirrup; his family still runs it, seven generations on. His son added the clock tower up the lane, so the whole town could share one time. The next track starts at Symi Square, down the bazaar and past the museum, at the one temple inside the walls you can touch.
long:
In front of the rose-pink mosque, find the small domed fountain standing on eight columns. They were taken from buildings older than the mosque, and the water is not for drinking. It is for washing hands, face and feet before prayer, and the way it was paid for is the way most of this town was paid for.

An Ottoman town did not run a water department. It ran on endowments. A family would lock away shops or orchards for ever, name a trustee, and let the rents pay for a mosque, a fountain, a teacher, a soup kitchen. The Orthodox church of Rhodes, on its heritage website, says it plainly: to a Muslim, building a public fountain was a benefit for the soul. The foundations register for eighteen eighty-five counted on this island forty-four mosques, fifty water fountains and twenty cemeteries held that way. And exactly one library. It is the one across the lane, and it is still running.

Hafiz Ahmed Agha was born around seventeen forty in Asgourou, a village four kilometres south of here, and served two sultans as chief equerry. On the twenty-sixth of February seventeen ninety-two he signed his foundation deed in Istanbul, and the next year the library opened with eight hundred and twenty-eight manuscripts, the foundation says, and eight hundred and six still carry his seal. The rents still pay the bills, and the trustee today is his seventh-generation descendant, Tarik Tuten, who uses the Arabic word for an endowment, waqf, and says: "No other waqf like this, let alone a library, still exists under the original family's care. It's a miracle it survives." The groundskeeper, Yusuf, has kept the courtyard for forty years on those rents.

The founder's son, Ahmed Fethi Pasha, marshal of the imperial arsenal, put the clock tower you can see fifty metres up the lane, between eighteen fifty and eighteen fifty-two, and beside it a house for the timekeeper. A school followed the year after. The clock came from Edward Prior, Chambers and Company of London and drove all four dials. The timekeeper worked out the five daily prayer times from the sun, and the town took its time from him. That is how an Ottoman town made time public: as a pious act, out of one family's rents. If you climb it with Rob for his birthday drink, you are climbing inside that act of piety, a tower built so that a whole town could agree what time it was.

Your address here was not a street. It was a mahalle, a neighbourhood named for the prayer-house at its centre, where the families who prayed together lived together. The census of eighteen thirty-one found twenty-three Muslim neighbourhoods and two Jewish ones inside these walls, some two thousand names on the rolls of the Muslim quarters alone, and the names are a social map: the Judge's quarter, the Bootmaker Ali Agha's, and the one called With Cupboards, after the wooden panelling the Ottomans fitted over the walls of an old church down by the Red Gate. The judge's court took crime and trade for everyone; for marriages and wills the Greeks went to their Metropolitan and the Jews to their rabbis, and the non-Muslims paid a poll tax in place of military service.

Now the unusual part. In nineteen twenty-three, when Greece and Turkey exchanged most of their Muslims and Christians by treaty, this island was Italian, and the same treaty said so. The exchange passed it by, and so did the protections written in for the Muslims who stayed in Greece. The island's Muslims simply stayed, and became Greek citizens in nineteen forty-seven. There are two to four thousand of them today. One mosque, Ibrahim Pasha, near where you ate lunch, is in regular use, licensed only in twenty nineteen; its caretaker's family has been here since fifteen twenty-six, and he says it gets crowded on Fridays. The call to prayer stays inside the building. Of six hundred plots the endowments held in nineteen twenty-five, the community says around sixty remain. And for decades, the anthropologist Kira Kaurinkoski found, official guides here were instructed not to mention the Ottoman past. Consider it mentioned.

When you are ready, the bazaar runs back downhill to the square, then north past the museum to Symi Square, where the only temple you can touch inside the walls lies in a fenced heap, in a city that once owned three thousand statues.

title: A Second City of Clubs
short: Stop at the fence and look through it at the column drums and the low platform they fell from: a temple of Aphrodite, third century before Christ. Notice where she was put, with the trading harbour on one side of you and the old war harbour on the other. Between two harbours she was the goddess of safe landing, the one a sailor thanked when the anchor held, and many of those sailors were foreigners, in this city but not of it. They could not vote or own land, so they built a second city out of clubs, about two hundred of them, which fed them, crowned them and buried them by subscription. Just north of you is the gate the Italians cut; the next track tells you when and why.
long:
Stop at the fence and look through it at the column drums and the low platform they fell from, a temple from the third century before Christ. The archaeologists give it to Aphrodite; notice where she was put: the trading harbour on one side of you, the old war harbour on the other. Put between two harbours, she was surely less the goddess of love than of safe landing. She is the first in a line of sea-guardians on this shore. Saint Nicholas of the sailors, in the fort at the mole's end, and the Virgin's cathedral on the waterfront across the harbour mouth from it, are the ones who came after her. The prayer changes; the shore does not.

The trading harbour filled this city with people who were in it but not of it. They could not vote, could not own land, could not be buried as citizens. So they built a second city out of clubs. Rhodes has left about two hundred of them in stone, and one Rhodian's name is attached to no fewer than twenty-three of them; he cannot have been at all the dinners. Many were named for gods, so there were Aphrodisiasts for the goddess in front of you and Haliasts for the Sun. One club's roll lists Ephesians, Antiochians and Alexandrians, a Phrygian and a Knidian, alongside several Rhodians.

What they did was pool money. In one hundred and eighty-five before Christ, in the cemetery south of this city, thirty-six members of a club of the Samothracian gods, Hermes and the Panathenaia bought a shared grave for about a thousand drachmas, and the stone says they promised to give voluntarily money for the price of the place, and they did pay. It is dated, naturally, by the priest of the Sun, Nikasagoras, whose name was that year's name across the island. A building fund from about ten years earlier lists Xouthos of Antioch at twenty drachmas and Dromon of Cappadocia at five, plus doors. The museum you were in this morning, whose square you have just crossed, keeps a stone on which a Phoenician called Abd-Melqart calls himself, in Greek, Heraclides of Citium. That is the immigrant experience in one object. The people in this city but not of it today are the season's workers; last year more than a quarter of Greek hotels hired from outside the Union.

The year the city died politically was forty-two before Christ. Cassius, Caesar's assassin, came for it. The Rhodians chose to fight, and fell when sympathisers inside opened the small gates. Cassius took his seat on the tribunal and planted a spear beside it, summoned about fifty citizens by name and had them killed, and ordered all the gold and silver in the city brought to him, with death for anyone who hid it, a tenth to informers, and freedom to any slave who told. He emptied the temples too, the historian Cassius Dio says, with the exception of the chariot of the Sun, which is probably Lysippus's bronze Helios in his four-horse chariot. Who decided now? A Roman with a spear beside his chair.

What Rome left was a free city on paper, and the freedom was a dial. In the year forty-four after Christ the Rhodians lost it for impaling some Romans; nine years later a sixteen-year-old Nero won it back. The best witness to daily life under Rome is a visiting orator, a different Dio, who came to scold the Rhodians about statues. Pliny reports three thousand still standing here in his day, and when a Roman wanted the honour of one, the chief magistrate merely pointed his finger at the first statue that met his eyes, had the old inscription removed and a new name engraved. Then he holds up a mirror: your remaining silent as you watch the games, your applauding by making a clucking sound with your lips. Anyone landing here, he says, knew at once he had not come to some city of Syria or of Cilicia.

Just north of you is the gate the Italians cut; the next track tells you when and why.

title: The Small Citizenship
short: Stand under the arch. The Italians cut this opening through the medieval wall in nineteen twenty-four and named it Liberty, for themselves, as liberators of Rhodes from the Turks. Then came a citizenship: you kept your religious law, you owed no military service, and you had no vote that reached Rome. People called it the small citizenship; the large kind was a reward for cooperating with the Italians. Through the arch is the new town, in red-orange fake stone imitating the Knights' masonry. That is where the food market was sent in nineteen twenty-six, so the walled town could become a bazaar for visitors. It still is. Follow the water north to the two columns with the stag and the doe.
long:
Stop under the arch, one foot in the medieval town and one on the pavement outside, because this opening is the seam between two cities and the seam has a date. The Italians cut it through the wall in nineteen twenty-four and named it the Gate of Liberty, for themselves, as the liberators of Rhodes from the Turks. Look through it. Across the road is a new town in red-orange fake stone imitating the masonry of the Knights, and the long low ring across the square, still closed for restoration, is the market that replaced the one inside the walls. All of it was built to organise the people behind you.

Italy landed at Kallithea Bay down the coast before dawn on the fourth of May, nineteen twelve, and marched into the walled town next morning through the Red Gate you passed by the Jewish quarter. The Greeks of ten islands met on Patmos that June and proclaimed a state of their own, hoping to join Greece, and were ignored. Italy called its stay provisional until a treaty of nineteen twenty-three made it permanent. The islands became a possession, neither a province nor a colony, one historian says: too far away to be Italy and too white, as the age put it, to be Africa. The town, by the census of nineteen twenty-two, was three big communities: six and a half thousand Muslims, five and a half thousand Orthodox and four thousand Jews.

So they sorted people. A decree of October nineteen twenty-five gave the islanders a citizenship of their own: you kept your personal law for marriage and inheritance, you owed no military service, and had no political rights or duties in Rome. People called it the small citizenship. The large kind was a reward for cooperating with the authorities, and without it you could not even join the Fascist Party; asked in nineteen twenty-nine whether islanders might join, Governor Lago judged the time unripe. Lago ran the place the Ottoman way, through communities: he kept the old civil code and the religious courts, let towns elect their own mayors, and encouraged Italians to marry local Greeks; the Church of Rhodes says a mixed marriage came with automatic conversion to Catholicism and money to sweeten it. His successor, De Vecchi, tried to make Italians instead. In nineteen thirty-seven every mayor was replaced by an appointed podestà, and Italian took over the schools; Greek was optional, without books, and only for the youngest children. That spring De Vecchi banned the Venetokleion schoolboys' berets, and the police reported boys weeping and kissing the caps. When the headmaster ordered them to the fascist festival of the birthday of Rome in April, an eighteen-year-old stood up and asked, Mister Headmaster, did you not always tell us that we are Greeks? The headmaster was dismissed, seven boys arrested, three expelled from every school in the islands, and the school shut until nineteen forty-three.

Shopping was organised too. When the new market opened in nineteen twenty-six, the administration ordered every merchant still selling food inside the medieval town to leave at once; the Italian paper, the Messenger of Rhodes, explained that the old market was scattered through the walled city, impossible to inspect and short of water, and promised visitors in its place one of those characteristic oriental bazaars. So the farmers went outside the walls, the inside became a souvenir bazaar, and the street you climbed after lunch, and have just walked back down, is that decision, still running. And here is the part I like. A regime that claimed to have rescued Rhodes from five centuries of Ottoman rule restored more than thirty mosques and fitted out a working Turkish bath, ordering carpets and costume from Turkey, and insisting that at least two bath-masseurs, between twenty and fifty and in good moral and physical health, always be on hand. The tourists came to look, not to bathe. The Ottoman town was stripped inside the walls and restaged outside them as scenery.

Two years after the berets, the same administration raised two columns at the mouth of the harbour ahead of you and put a bronze stag and doe on top. Every age has decided for itself where the sun god's statue stood, and those columns are the answer the Italians built. Walk north along the water to them; that is where the fallen god gets measured.

title: Measuring the God
short: Look across the water from one column to the other: a bronze stag, a bronze doe, sixty-two metres between them, and no, the Colossus never stood on them. Pliny says few men could get their arms round the fallen god's thumb, so men were trying; a chronicler measured him in nine hundred camels; this town measures him in deer. And the water itself is what the Rhodians gave things to: a chariot for the Sun once a year in antiquity, and every sixth of January still, just back along the quay, a cross thrown in for a young man to bring back. Every age measures the Colossus with its own instruments. Now walk the mole to the fort and turn round at the end.
long:
Stand at the foot of one of the two columns and look across the water to the other. A bronze stag on one of them, a bronze doe on the other, sixty-two metres of harbour mouth between them. Every guide will tell you the Colossus stood with a foot on each. It did not; the columns simply stand where an old picture needs two feet.

The statue broke at the knees and lay where it fell for centuries, and the question is who came to look. Pliny says few men could get their arms round the thumb, which means men were trying: for three hundred years visitors hugged a fallen god to find out how big he was, and saw, where the limbs had broken, the rock inside that steadied him. Eight hundred years after the casting a writer who goes by the name of Philo was still measuring it on paper, five hundred talents of bronze and three hundred of iron, and said that on the earth a second sun now stood facing the first. By the late thirteen hundreds there was nothing left to see.

Then the camels. A medieval chronicler, writing of the year six hundred and fifty-three or four, has nine hundred of them carry the bronze away. Scholars do not believe the sale; notice only what the number is doing. Nine hundred camels at two hundred kilos each comes to something like a hundred and eighty tonnes, about a dozen times the bronze Philo says went into the statue. It is the last hug of the thumb: the god measured in the largest unit the teller owned.

Now back to the deer. Nobody has quite pinned down who put them up: a Rhodes newspaper says the Italians in nineteen thirty-nine, another account gives only a year, nineteen forty-seven, and no sculptor at all. What is certain is that a town which, in March nineteen forty-eight, raised the Greek flag in front of the fascist party house along this quay, the fascist symbols already chiselled off, the King looking on, and the building now its town hall, left the deer standing, and they are the island's badge now. Guides say deer were brought to Rhodes to drive out the snakes, on an oracle's advice or by the Knights. No ancient writer says so. One of the island's old names did mean snake island, and Diodorus tells the ancient story plainly: the island crawled with snakes, an oracle of Apollo told the Rhodians to send for a Thessalian called Phorbas, and Phorbas killed the snakes, settled here, and after his death was honoured as a hero. The oracle that once sent for a hero now sends for a deer. The Rhodian fallow deer are real, and genetically a line of their own. So a town whose Greeks, three and a half centuries after the conquest, were still walking out of their own walled centre at sunset, took a small, gentle, native animal for its badge, and left it standing where the pagan giant was supposed to have straddled the harbour. Every age measures the Colossus with its own instruments and plants it where its own harbour is.

Now look at the water, because the water is what the Rhodians gave things to. A Roman dictionary-maker named Festus, explaining why Romans sacrificed a horse in October, reached for a foreign parallel: the Rhodians, who every year throw into the sea four-horse chariots consecrated to the Sun, because he is said to be carried round the world in such a chariot. That is the whole of it: no date, no colour of horses, not even whether it belonged to the Halieia, the city's games for the Sun. The rest you can work out for yourself: he goes down into this same sea every evening on the far side of this point, and climbs out of it every morning off the Turkish coast; once a year the city sent a chariot down into it after him.

A hundred and fifty metres back along the waterfront stands the church of the Annunciation, and on the sixth of January the town still walks from it to the water. In twenty twenty-five Metropolitan Kyrillos blessed the waters on a platform behind the church, and a young man named Michalis Mavridis came up with the cross; in January this year the programme had the Municipal Philharmonic and a detachment of soldiers walking with the cross from the church to the pier again. Nobody can show that one rite descends from the other. But it is the one ceremony left in which this town gives something to the sea and takes it back. The pattern survives; the god's name did not.

Now walk out along the mole to the fort, and at the end turn round and look back. The next track asks where you put a god.

title: Where You Put a God
short: Stand with the round fort at your back and the small closed harbour in front of you. The question here is not where the Colossus stood but where a city puts its god: in his own precinct, because the precinct was an office, and the priest of the Sun named the year. And the word kolossos once meant a magical figure of any size that could hold a god; at Thera the whole town watched wax ones burn as its settlers swore their oath. One word for a wax figure that burned in an oath and a bronze god the height of a ten-storey building. Walk back along the mole to the floating decks by the market.
long:
Stand at the end of the mole with the round fort at your back and the small closed harbour in front of you. Behind the fort, to the north across the strait, is the coast of Turkey. This is the traditional spot for the Colossus, and nobody knows. The better question is where a city puts its god.

Three places claim it: under this fort, on the acropolis hill to the south-west with the re-erected columns, and on the small hill under the Palace, where the Sun's priests left their dedications. Nobody has dug. But the two candidates scholars now favour, the Palace hill and the acropolis, share one assumption, and it is why they have left this mole: a votive belongs in the god's own precinct, and the precinct was an office. The priest of the Sun named the year on every decree and every wine jar. You put the god where his office was. The face you saw in the museum this morning, drilled round the brow for metal rays, is well over a century younger than the Colossus and from another statue, and nobody has published where it was found; it is still the closest you will come to the face they were buying.

Then there is the word. A kolossos, Nathan Badoud reminds us, was originally a magical figure, not defined by its size, that could hold a god or a mortal inside it. When Thera sent settlers to found Cyrene, so a later inscription says, the whole town, children included, watched wax kolossoi burn as the settlers swore never to abandon the colony, and cursed any oath-breaker to melt away like the wax. By the time Rhodes built hers the word already meant, plainly, a statue bigger than a man. One word for a wax figure burned in an oath and a bronze god the height of a ten-storey building.

Now the water in front of you. This was the closed war harbour; the big harbour where your ship lies was the open market. One basin for citizens with oars, one for foreigners with cargo. Some of the dockyards here were secret; to spy on them, or even to walk inside, was death. A trihemiolia, the Rhodian pirate-hunter, carried a hundred and forty-four men, a hundred and twenty of them at the oars. Diodorus counted six thousand citizens under arms in the siege; forty such ships would have swallowed most of them. That arithmetic explains Strabo's strangest line about Rhodes. The well-to-do fed the needy, he says, by an ancestral custom, so that the poor man receives his sustenance and the city does not run short of useful men, and in particular for the manning of the fleets. The custom ran on liturgies, public duties the rich paid for in person. Welfare as a naval budget wearing the clothes of charity. The families who captained the ships also held the priesthood of the Sun; Vincent Gabrielsen calls them the naval aristocracy of Rhodes.

That coast was theirs as well. The villages on the near shore were Rhodian demes; their people came over to hold priesthoods on this island; in one hundred and eighty-eight before Christ Rome handed Rhodes the mainland behind it, Caria and Lycia, then took it back twenty-one years later for staying neutral in the wrong war. Today that shore is Turkey, a ferry ride and a customs post away. The Sun ran their clock too: the Antikythera Mechanism has a dial of games, and in its fourth-year slot sits the Halieia, the games of the Sun; that spelling, Paul Iversen argues, is found almost nowhere but Rhodes, the first link in his case that the machine was made on this island.

The Knights built the fort over a chapel of Saint Nicholas, the sailors' patron. What ties it to the dead is fourteen eighty. After the failed assault, seven hundred bodies covered the rocks and the mole; the Turks were allowed to bury them in an immense pit facing the fort; the bones, uncovered shortly before eighteen eighty-one, were reburied in the Ottoman cemetery across the water. Count the guardians on this shore: Aphrodite at the little temple by Symi Square, Helios on this mole if he was ever here, Nicholas in the fort, and the Annunciation on the quay, behind which, every sixth of January, the cross goes into this harbour and the young men dive for it. Four guardians, one job.

Walk back along the mole, past the windmills, to the floating decks by the closed market; the next track there is about how a Greek celebrates, and who pays for it.

title: Chronia Polla
short: Go up to the top deck and look along the quay, where later the town will come out for its evening walk. Today is Rob's birthday, and in Greece that is the lesser feast. The day that counts is the name day, the feast of the saint you were named for, and it was kept as an open house: friends dropped in, said chronia polla, many years, and the one celebrating fed them. Now people ring ahead, but the shape holds and birthdays borrow it, so the wish today is chronia polla, not happy birthday, and the drinks are on Rob. Later, the way back runs along this water, past a gate named for Paul and the stump of a tower an earthquake broke, and the return track waits there.
long:
Climb to the top deck and take a seat at the rail where you can see both the town quay beside you and, across the water, the windmills on the mole and the fort at its end. This is the stretch of waterfront where Rhodes comes out in the evening for its volta, the slow walk along the water at sundown, and you are here a few hours ahead of it. Today is Rob's birthday, and the first thing to know about a birthday in Greece is that it is the lesser feast.

The day that counts is the name day, the feast of the saint you were named for. Ask a Greek friend and they will tell you a name day matters more than a birthday, and matters more the older you get. The Church, for its part, treats a birthday as the anniversary of your arrival on earth and would rather you did not make a party of it. A name day runs the other way round from a birthday: nobody surprises you, because the calendar is public, and you are the one who does the giving. The house used to be simply open; lately the invitations go out first, but the shape has not changed. Friends and relatives come to wish you well and leave a small gift, and the one being celebrated does the feeding: coffee, sweets, drinks, whatever is on the table. The kerasma, the treat, comes from the celebrant. The wish is chronia polla, many years. Not happy birthday. Many years. So the rule for this deck is simple. Everyone says chronia polla, and Rob pays.

Names here are inherited more than chosen. The eldest grandson takes his grandfather's name, the eldest granddaughter her grandmother's, so the same saints come round through a family every second generation, and a family's calendar is really its tree. Someone named for a hero instead of a saint, an Achilleas, an Odysseas, has no name day at all and borrows All Saints' Sunday, the Sunday after Pentecost. And Rhodes has a name that exists nowhere else, because it is a vow. A woman who wants a child climbs, barefoot by most accounts, to the little chapel of the Virgin at Tsambika on the east coast, on the eve of the eighth of September, a little over three weeks ago, and the child who follows is called Tsambikos or Tsambika. The name is the receipt.

And the thirtieth of September? It belongs to Gregory the Illuminator, the enlightener of Greater Armenia, and a few Armenian martyrs nobody in Greece is named for. A quiet day. Even Greeks called Grigoris keep their feast in January instead. Almost nobody in Greece has a name day today, which makes Rob, in Greek terms, about the only celebrant on the quay, and the treat is his.

Look down at the quay before you go. The Jewish museum remembers this waterfront, which it calls the square, as the place where in the Italian years the young of the quarter came to look at each other, "young men and women walking from one end of the square to the other, backwards and forwards, crossing and crisscrossing each other exchanging silent looks day after day." That walk still happens along this water in the evening, and the ship sails before it begins, so you are seeing the town just before it comes out to look at itself.

Whenever you are ready, the way back is along this water, out past a gate named for Paul and the stump of a tower an earthquake took down in eighteen sixty-three, and the return track picks you up there.

title: Who Ran the Island When
short: The broken stump out at the head of this mole, beside the harbour light, was a tower of the Knights; the bastion at its root is the Gate of Saint Paul, with the apostle in relief and a pope's arms. Turn and look across the harbour to the ship. That gangway has been a toll gate for twenty-two centuries. In one hundred and sixty-four before Christ a Rhodian envoy told the Roman Senate the harbour dues, once farmed for a million drachmas, now fetched a hundred and fifty thousand. The Knights sold the customs to a Genoese, the Ottomans to contractors, and since July of last year every cruise passenger pays a landing levy at that gangway. Walk back along the mole.
long:
The broken stump out at the head of this mole, beside the harbour light, was a tower of the Knights. Look back along the mole to the bastion at its root: that is the Gate of Saint Paul, and your story starts there. On the tower over the gate the Knights set a relief of the apostle, sword in one hand and Gospel in the other, and the arms of Pope Sixtus the Fourth, the pope of the fourteen eighty siege: two carvings, one constitution. The Order ran this island as a sovereign state, a monastery with a mint and a fleet, but it answered to Rome: in thirteen nineteen the Pope unmade two Grand Masters and installed a third. The Acts of the Apostles say only that Paul's ship called at Rhodes; tradition, not the Bible, lands him at Lindos, in a bay below the altar where the sons of the Sun sacrificed without fire.

The last handover took five years. When Italy's armistice came in nineteen forty-three the Germans took the island within days, and the winter of nineteen forty-four to forty-five was famine, a catastrophe you will pass no monument to today. The bishop's first telegram for help went not to a government but to the Patriarch of Alexandria and the Archbishop of Athens: "The people of Rhodes in agreement with the Red Cross are agonizingly awaiting sacks of flour." Hunger sorted people by where they had kin: about four thousand of the nine thousand Dodecanese Muslims crossed to Turkey and were sent back in nineteen forty-five; Greeks who fled ended up in makeshift British refugee camps on Kasos and Karpathos. When the Germans surrendered, the British kept the Italian tax system, minus its fascist clauses, fed the town from Red Cross soup kitchens, and in the spring of nineteen forty-seven handed the island to a Greek rear admiral. On the seventh of March nineteen forty-eight the Greek flag went up in front of the Italian government buildings on Mandraki, with the King present, once the fasces and Mussolini's statues of Caesar and Octavian had been taken away. It is still a holiday across the Dodecanese, with a parade along the esplanade the Italians laid out for mass gatherings.

Every regime taxed the gangway. In one hundred and sixty-four before Christ the envoy Astymedes told the Roman Senate that the harbour dues, once farmed for a million drachmas, now fetched a hundred and fifty thousand, because Rome had made Delos a free port; a republic became a client. The Knights farmed their customs to the Genoese Tobias Lomelino, who bought the farm year after year in the fourteen seventies. The Ottomans sold the taxes to contractors who took back up to five times what they paid. And since July of last year every cruise passenger stepping ashore in Greece pays a landing levy, which the ship settles on your behalf every quarter.

If you want the whole history of who ran this island in two words, they are on a coin. After the Crusaders took Constantinople in twelve hundred and four, a local magnate named Leo Gabalas held Rhodes on his own account and struck coins that say Caesar on one face and servant of the emperor on the other. The republic of the sailors kept every king as a friend and none as a master; the Knights minted their own money and answered to the Pope; for three centuries the Ottoman governor here answered to the admiral of the fleet, and for most of four, as Tozer saw in eighteen eighty-six, the Greeks who kept the shops inside these walls were "obliged to quit the place at sunset". Sovereign on one face, somebody's servant on the other.

Four questions have followed you round the walls today: who decided, who paid, who could own, who could sleep inside. Every regime answered them differently, but the sharpest mark of belonging has always been the walled town after dark: a curfew bell and a lantern then, a resident's car permit and a holiday flat's registry number now. Walk back along the mole and round the quay. The ship is across the water from you, and its gangway is the last toll gate of the day.

title: B-side: When the Island Breaks
short: Stand on the floor of the ditch, thirty metres of grass between the two walls, and near you a stack of stone cannonballs: ammunition, then rubble, then ornament, now the one thing in this park nobody planted, and who stacked them is anyone's guess. Rhodes breaks about once a century, and each time two questions come round: who pulls the neighbours out, and who pays for the walls. Rescue is whoever is already here; rebuilding is a sovereign somewhere else, popes once, Brussels now. On the south-east stretch, between the Saint John bastion and the harbour, the ditch opens into a theatre where one August night the town heard swing tunes for free on the old siege ground.
long:
Find a place on the floor of the ditch where you can see both walls at once, thirty metres of grass between them, and near you a stack of stone cannonballs. They have been ammunition, then rubble, then ornament, and now they are the one thing in this park nobody planted, and who stacked them is anyone's guess. About once a century this ground answers the same question: what happens when the island breaks.

The first break came nine months after the Ottoman siege lifted in August fourteen eighty. At three in the morning on the third of May fourteen eighty-one the shock came, a magnitude of about seven, enough to crack the Palace and to raise a small wave that still tore a large ship from its moorings; that ship, or another, later ran onto a reef and went down with all hands. The old catalogues say thirty thousand dead, a number nobody can check; the damage was real, and what you are standing in is the answer to it and to the siege before it: the ditch, the islands of earth and stone in it, the bastions above you, rebuilt between fourteen eighty-one and fifteen twenty. The Order of Saint John was, among other things, an insurance company. Its commanderies across Europe each sent a yearly remittance, the responsions; in thirteen twenty-nine the Venetian Marino Sanudo grumbled that an Order taking a hundred and eighty thousand florins a year from those alone could not put two or three galleys to sea. And the pope signed for his share: over Saint Paul's Gate, at the Mandraki end of this ditch, the arms of Sixtus the Fourth still sit beside the saint, as near as the Knights came to a donor's plaque.

The second break came twice in one autumn. The great Cretan earthquake of October eighteen fifty-six reached this island in the small hours; sixty people died here and the coastline lifted. Twenty-five days later lightning struck the bell tower of the old church of Saint John beside the Palace and fired a store of gunpowder in its cellars that the Ottoman authorities did not know about. At least two hundred died. The Ottoman answer was a school on the rubble, and the Palace, used for a time as a convict prison, stayed a half-ruin for eighty years until the Italians rebuilt it; today the walls are kept up with European money.

This ditch has also held people. The Italians laid out these gardens where, the old accounts say, there had been orchards under both the Knights and the Turks, clearing the Ottoman graveyards that had grown up against the walls and, on the stretch ahead of you, the Jewish cemetery, whose families could move a grave if they could pay for it. The traveller Henry Tozer, walking here in eighteen eighty-six, saw a Turkish one just outside the moat, where, he wrote, lay the bones of the besiegers who fell during the siege; he can only mean fifteen twenty-two. After Italy attacked Greece in October nineteen forty, the Orthodox Metropolis of Rhodes records Greek-citizen teachers imprisoned in the old city moat, and a local history of the island says Governor De Vecchi kept a camp for Greek nationals in these trenches.

The oldest answer is the one Rhodes wrote down. In three hundred and five before Christ, before the great siege began, the assembly voted the terms in advance: public burial for anyone who fell, their parents and children maintained from the public treasury, their daughters given dowries at the public cost, and, in the historian Diodorus's words, to buy from their masters any slaves who proved themselves brave men in the battle, and to emancipate and enfranchise them. The ancient city drew the circle of who counted before the disaster, wide enough to take in its slaves. Every regime since has drawn it during the disaster: by which church you gave to, which passport you held, or, in the wildfires of two thousand and twenty-three, which hotel you had booked.

On the south-east stretch, between the Saint John bastion and the great round bastion at the harbour corner, the ditch opens into the Melina Mercouri theatre, where one August night the town put on a free evening of Manolis Chiotis's swing tunes. The siege ground is the town's living room now, and nobody sleeps in it against their will. The ditch ends either by the port, a few minutes from the ship, or at Mandraki under the pope's coat of arms.

title: B-side: The Business of Strangers
short: Stand in the small rotunda, the round pavilion with the six arched gates. Italy landed on this beach at four in the morning on the fourth of May nineteen twelve, and seventeen years later built a spa on the same shore, with the King of Italy in the front row. The historian Valerie McGuire found that the water visitors took was bottled nearby and drunk, which makes the pool under this dome mostly a photograph. This island's oldest trade is strangers: bathers, enemies who need a neutral room to talk in, and, in one bad week of July twenty twenty-three, nineteen thousand people who needed a bed. On the road back, watch for the row of cemeteries: the Italians sorted even the dead by faith.
long:
Stand in the small rotunda, the round pavilion with the six arched gates, and look out at the water. Italy landed on this beach at four in the morning on the fourth of May nineteen twelve, unopposed, and the town surrendered the next day. Seventeen years later the Italian governor built a spa on the site, and the King of Italy, Victor Emmanuel the Third, came to open it on the first of July nineteen twenty-nine. Together with the Hotel of the Roses on the town shore, now the casino, this was Italy bringing mass tourism to Rhodes. The spa's own history claims Hippocrates and Herodotus for its pedigree; treat that as advertising. And the historian Valerie McGuire adds a deflating detail: the water the visitors actually took was bottled nearby and drunk, which makes the little pool under the dome you are standing beneath mostly a photograph. Today the town hires the place out for weddings. So a beach where soldiers came ashore became a place people pay to lie down. That is the island's oldest business: taking strangers in.

It takes them in for talking, too. In January nineteen forty-nine the United Nations mediator Ralph Bunche, an American, opened the armistice talks between Egypt and Israel on Rhodes; the Hotel of the Roses says the agreement was signed under its roof, on the twenty-fourth of February. He won the Nobel Peace Prize for it, and twenty years later American and Soviet diplomats were still arguing over a Rhodes formula: a go-between, separate rooms to begin with, and one table once the parties were ready. Nothing could be more Rhodian. For nearly a hundred and forty years the ancient republic fought beside Rome and never signed a treaty with her, because, as Polybius puts it, they wished none of the kings and princes to despair of gaining their help and alliance, and so did not desire to run in harness with Rome. Neutrality was the product. Every king was a potential customer.

And when the money stops, the island takes people in for nothing. On the eighteenth of July twenty twenty-three a fire started above the village of Laerma and ran for a week towards the south-east coast. Within three days there was a state of emergency, Laerma was emptied, and then the coast villages below it, Pefki, Lindos, Kalathos; by the end about nineteen thousand people had been moved, two thousand of them off the beaches by boat. The fire service called it the largest evacuation the island had ever seen. Where do nineteen thousand people sleep? This town alone has something like thirty thousand hotel beds. A hotel is a building designed to absorb strangers at scale, and in a crisis it is the spare room of the whole island; the Knights' hospital in the old town, this spa and the all-inclusive down the road are one trade. On the second of August the emergency was lifted and the Ministry of Tourism offered the evacuated visitors free accommodation. The visitors, notice. And eight years earlier, in April twenty fifteen, a migrant boat struck a reef off this same eastern shore with ninety-six people aboard. Three died. The other ninety-three were got out in shallow water, and the photographs the papers ran that week showed people from the shore standing waist-deep, passing survivors hand to hand.

The spa sold water. Last winter a hydrologist, Elisavet Feloni, told the island's newspaper that Rhodes has entered a water-alert zone, that demand, above all the tourists', now exceeds what the rain can give back, and almost no rain falls here in July, August or September, so you are standing at the driest point of the island's year, in a spa built to sell the stuff.

On the road back you will pass, in a row, a Catholic cemetery, a Muslim one and a Jewish one, planned from nineteen twenty-five by the architect who drew the Hotel of the Roses, with the Orthodox behind and the Commonwealth war cemetery across the road. The twentieth century sorted its dead by faith and by army: the Catholic ground keeps its soldiers in a half-circle of niches under one tall cross, and the war cemetery opposite took in sixty-five graves from Kos when that ground closed in nineteen fifty-seven; a hundred and forty-two lie there under the Commonwealth's care. Keep to the time you were given for the taxi; the next track, if you take it, waits on the hill above the town.

title: B-side: Three Cities, One Contract
short: You are standing by four columns on a ridge, and below you is the long straight of a stadium. In four hundred and eight before Christ the island's three old towns, Lindos, Ialysos and Kameiros, stopped being three states and poured their people into one new city of identical blocks. The trick: they never dissolved. They became the three tribes of the new state, and a household belonged at once to its village, its tribe and the city that kept the fleet. Ask a Rhodian where they are from and you may well hear the village before the island. Look down at the stadium, where the city would have run the Sun's games, and think of one boxing family from Ialysos whose name is now on the airport.
long:
You are standing by four columns on a ridge, and below you is the long straight of a stadium. Look north along the ridge to the summit, then east over the town to the two harbours. Everything between here and the water was one city laid out by agreement.

Diodorus gives the founding one sentence, under the year we call four hundred and eight before Christ: the people of the island left the cities of Ialysos, Lindos and Kameiros and settled in one city, the one now called Rhodes. Three separate states agreed to stop being three. The blocks were identical, three houses to each, drains underneath. Identical blocks mean allotment: three populations that had run their own affairs, measured out and mixed street by street.

Here is the trick. The three cities did not dissolve. They became the three tribes of the new state, Lindia, Kamiris and Ialysia, competing against each other at the festivals of the new capital. Under the tribes ran the demes, the villages, so a citizen was formally of such-and-such a village. Under the demes ran something older still, small units of land and their local rites, that the new system covered over but never abolished. Soon after three hundred and twenty-five before Christ the people of Kameiros resolved to carve the names of all their land-units on a stone in Athena's temple, the contractor chosen by lowest bid. So a household belonged at once to its plot and its local shrine, to its village for registration, to its tribe for priesthoods and games, and to the city for the assembly, the fleet and the law. Nested belonging, four layers deep. That is the invention, more than the grid.

Who decided, and who ate? Somewhere below you, never found, is the theatre where the assembly and the courts met. Cicero has Scipio describe the arrangement: the same men were senators and private citizens by turns, for certain months each, paid for both, and decided capital cases in the theatre and the council house alike. Strabo is blunt that the rule was not democratic, but by an ancestral custom the well-to-do supplied the poor with provisions, so that the city never ran short of men to row. The navy was the welfare state. A rich man's duty was to feed rowers, and a poor man's was to row.

No ancient text names this track, but it is the stadium the city has, so picture the Sun's games, the Halieia, run here: the procession coming up from the town, the sacrifice, then the runners on this straight. The family to know is Diagoras of Ialysos, Olympic boxing champion in four hundred and sixty-four before Christ, whose three sons and two grandsons were all Olympic victors. When two of his sons won at Olympia on the same day, Cicero says, a Spartan came up to the old man and told him: die, Diagoras, for you are not going to climb up to heaven. His daughter Kallipateira went to Olympia disguised as a trainer to watch her son, was discovered, and, Pausanias says, was acquitted for the family's record, after which trainers had to strip too. Today the airport and one of the football clubs are named Diagoras.

One last pair. Around six hundred before Christ Cleobulus governed Lindos and left the maxim moderation is best. Athenaeus preserves a song Rhodian children sang from door to door, asking the rich house for cake, wine and cheese, threatening to carry off the door, or the little wife, if refused, and ending: now open, open the door for the swallow, we are not old men, but only children. Athenaeus says Cleobulus started the collection when there was need of money. Redistribution disguised as a game. His daughter Cleobulina made the wise men guess: I have seen a man with fire fasten bronze on another. A doctor's heated cupping glass. Plutarch's Thales says her father's rule grew milder because of her.

The municipality still publishes four hundred and eight before Christ as the city's birthday, so Rob is sharing his with it. From here you can see the small hill under the Palace, where the most recent book on the Colossus puts the Sun's sanctuary and his statue, though nobody has ever dug to check, and beyond it the harbour where the ship is waiting. That is the whole city you walked today, in one look.
